translations.text: The elders of Ireland have drawn up, from the rules of the Scripture, a penitential of forgiveness and remedy for every sin, from small to great.
For the eight chief virtues, with their subdivisions, have been set down to heal and make whole the eight chief vices, together with whatever is born of them.
Moderation with patience against gluttony and drunkenness. Continence with chastity against lust and adultery.
Generosity with charity against greed; and goodwill of heart against envy and hatred. Meekness with gentleness against anger and strife.
Spiritual joy against worldly sorrow. Fear of death and decay against proud vainglory.
True humility with fear of the Lord against pride and arrogance.
These, then, are the names of the chief vices through which comes the death of the body and soul of every person, namely gluttony and lust, and so on.
These are the names of the subdivisions that are born of gluttony: unmeasured merriment, much talk, foolish singing,
vulgarity of thought, impurity of mind, tearful lamentation [?], drinking without control, drunkenness without restraint.
These, on the other hand, are the subdivisions that are born of patience: spiritual joy, beauty of body,
purity of soul, purposeful [?] silence, wise perception, abundance of understanding, reaching toward the mysteries of God.
These are the remedies for gluttony: measured fasting, contrition of heart, scantiness of meals, frequent self-examination [?], keeping vigil, a feast for the poor,
comforting everyone who is in sorrow, restriction to one meal a day, moderation [?] of special foods [?], patience in everything until it has been considered.
Luxuria (that is, lust) is the name of the second vice that kills a person's soul.
This is the offspring that is born of this vice: obscene words, ugly jesting, blindness of mind, instability of nature,
coarse talk, falling into decay [?], many counsels, promising without foundation, singing to attract, care for man, neglect of God.
This, then, is the virtue that has been appointed against this vice to destroy it: continence in chastity, with what is born of it, namely:
steadiness of counsel, steadfast speech, firmness against instability, true promising, fulfilling what is true,
contemplation of God, modesty of nature, strengthening of faith, hatred of this world, love of the world beyond.
These are the remedies for carnal lust: condemnation of gluttony, a measured meal, moderation in drink, avoidance of drunkenness,
hatred of concealment, subduing of nature, wariness in solitude, [?] in company, keeping close to elders,
avoidance of young people, turning to a book or to reading or to prayer, hatred of vulgarity with impure words,
a gracious mind with purity of speech, love of the reward so as to strive toward it, contemplation of the pains so as to avoid them.
Avaritia (that is, greed), then, is the name of the third vice that kills a person's soul.
This, then, is the offspring and lineage that is born of this vice: desire without moderation, great transgression [?] with despair, plundering without rest,
withholding without mercy, falsehood without restraint, perjury without limit, mockery of every good thing, delight in every evil,
blindness of mind, denial of natural feeling, oppressing every wretched person, enticing every strong person, greed for land, deceit concerning the soul.
This, then, is the virtue that has been appointed to fight against this vice: generosity with almsgiving, together with what is born of it, namely:
mercy with forgiveness, uprightness with truth, giving with gentleness, without pride, without loathing, without grudging [?],
compassion with zeal, without betrayal, without pretence, without boasting [?]; kindly goodwill with generosity, without falsehood, without perjury, without compulsion [?].
These, moreover, are the remedies for avarice: serving Christ's little ones, a feast for the poor, labour for one's sustenance, a mind set on poverty,
trust in blessing, foreseeing punishment, looking forward to reward, awaiting judgement before the face of the Creator on the Day of Judgement.
This is the name of the fourth vice that kills a person's soul.
This, then, is the offspring and progeny born of this vice: hatred of neighbours, grumbling at every good thing,
rejoicing at every evil, reproaching friends, sorrow at their being esteemed, joy at their being despised.
This is the virtue that has been appointed to fight against this vice:
kindly goodwill of heart without grudging [?], together with the virtues born of it, namely: brotherly love,
helping every neighbour, speaking well of everyone, hatred of slander, banishing grumbling, extolling every good thing,
lessening every evil, a gentle word, a compassionate mind toward every person, except where sin is deserved [?].
This is the name of the fifth vice that kills a person's soul.
Just as a blade through the body pierces a person's soul, so the point of anger pierces the soul and brings death to it.
This, then, is the offspring and progeny born of this vice of anger: manslaughter without humanity,
tormenting every neighbour without compassion, swelling of mind without subsiding, outcry of words without abating,
quarrelsomeness without ending, contention without reconciliation [?], reproaches without reflection, slander without restraint.
This, moreover, is the virtue that has been appointed to fight against this vice: meekness with gentleness, together with what is born of it, namely:
purity of heart, avoiding strife, a gentle word, restraining wrath, a docile nature, silence rather than talk,
patience in tribulation, hatred of slander, forgiveness without recrimination, kindly goodwill without pretence, [?] without grudging [?].
This is the name of the sixth vice that kills a person's soul.
There are two kinds of this vice: worldly sadness, with despair and unbelief, and godly sadness, with charity [?] and sound faith.
The one brings eternal joy in eternal life in heaven; the other brings eternal sorrow in the eternal torments of hell.
This, then, is the sadness that brings joy to the soul in heaven: the sadness that comes from weeping for sin with faith in forgiveness, and the sadness that comes from compassion
for every wretched person, every miserable person and every neighbour who is engaged in the work of sin and vice, and so falls into misery and poverty without faith and without repentance.
For whoever laments his own sins and the sins of his neighbour will be joyful with God in heaven.
That is why Christ says: 'Blessed are those who mourn now, for they shall be comforted.'
Worldly sadness, however, takes three forms, namely:
sadness and grief at being separated from carnal friends: missing their human company, and grieving for the love and affection they had,
or grief at being separated from one's wealth and earthly goods, or at being separated from wickedness, sin and one's carnal desires.
The second form of worldly sadness is grief and dejection over every desire a person has that goes unfulfilled [?], unless it is the will of God alone.
The third form of worldly sadness is grief and dejection over every good thing a person gets, for fear that it will be taken away from him
and that it will perish, and for fear of being parted from it even in the end [?], so that he is never without grief and sadness for as long as he lives,
and afterwards he goes on to everlasting grief, to eternal punishment without end.
These are the offspring and progeny born of worldly sadness: bitterness with irritability, lack of love with [?] (écmailte),
stinginess with [?] (foichlighe), too much talk with silence, the restless wandering of idleness without storing anything up [?], instability of nature,
restlessness of body, eagerness of mind for every base thing and for starting every evil, sluggishness and slackness towards every good,
dejection and faintheartedness in God's commandments, joy and vigour in the devil's works.
These are the remedies for worldly sadness: spiritual joy, with serenity of heart and mind, against worldly sadness;
earnest prayer with fasting and vigils against sluggishness and sleepiness; generosity with breadth of mind towards God against faintheartedness;
a set measure of labour and prayer against the restless wandering of idleness; faith with works; joy with gentleness against dejection and anger of mind.
This is the name of the seventh vice that kills a person's soul.
These are the offspring and progeny born of this vice: disobedience with obstinacy,
pride with arrogance, eagerness for strife, an unusual appearance, competing for rank without having the right to it,
boasting of good deeds, embellished speech, an eccentric appearance, freedom of the body, slavery of the soul.
These are the remedies prescribed to cure it: obedience without obstinacy, humility with modesty,
avoiding strife, an evenness without strangeness, learning from elders, stability of nature, a lowly mind, contemplation of God.
